notes: Slice 'dataprotection' covers 1970-1993: the invention of data protection statutes, independent commissioners and the fair information practice principles (FIPPs), plus the surveillance scandals and consumer protests that drove them. Method: every quote was captured from page text with tools/fetch-text.py and passed --check (108 source quotes, 94 unique URL+quote pairs, all FOUND); WebFetch paraphrases were never used as quotes. Non-English quotes are given in the original with a translation in the source note. Where official sites blocked scripts (OECD legalinstruments and oecd.org, coe.int and rm.coe.int, Légifrance, Lovdata, retsinformation.dk, legislation.govt.nz, LégisQuébec, CanLII, DOJ's PDF of the HEW report) the same primary text was read from a Wayback Machine snapshot (OECD 1980 guidelines page, Convention 108 treaty PDF, CoE Data Protection Day page), an official mirror (HHS/ASPE full text of the HEW report; CNIL's reproduction of Law 78-17 art. 1), or an official secondary account (NZ Law Commission, Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, Lov & Data). Dates: Hesse's act is dated 7 October 1970 and entered into force 13 October 1970; the Landtag readings were 8 July and 30 September 1970, and some official pages (BfDI) use 30 September - see myth-hesse-law-30-september-1970. Sweden's Data Act was issued 11 May 1973; Datainspektionen from 1 July 1973; permit provisions a year later. BDSG adopted 27 January 1977 (BfDI heading says 28 January; its text and the statute say 27). Coordinates are for the legislature, court, newsroom or organisation HQ as stated in each locationNote; Washington City Paper's 1987 office and the Privacy Protection Study Commission's office are city-centre approximations. The fipps array lists the HEW 1973 code (5, names editorial), the OECD 1980 basic principles (8, 1980 text, not the 2013 revision) and Convention 108 chapter II (Arts 5a-e, 6, 7, 8a-d), each text verbatim and checked. Not verified in primary form: Denmark's 1978 register acts (only a press list confirms Denmark legislated in 1978); the exact assent date of Québec's 1993 act (S.Q. 1993, c. 17); NZ Privacy Act assent date (only commencement 1 July 1993 confirmed); Convention 108's exact entry-into-force date (bpb gives 1985; 1 October 1985 per the treaty office, not read). No global count-of-laws series here by design (another slice).

events.title: Hesse passes the world's first data protection law
events.place: Hessischer Landtag (Stadtschloss), Wiesbaden, Hesse, West Germany
events.summary: The Datenschutzgesetz of the West German state of Hesse, dated 7 October 1970 (GVBl. I S. 625) after readings in the Landtag on 8 July and 30 September 1970, came into force on 13 October 1970. It set rules for the processing of personal data by state authorities and bodies under state supervision, and created the office of a data protection commissioner to oversee them. The occasion was the introduction of automated data processing in the Hessian administration.
events.significance: The word and the institution of 'data protection' begin here: a statute written because government computers, not snoopers at the door, had become the threat.

sources.institution: Hessisches Landesarchiv / Hessisches Hauptstaatsarchiv Wiesbaden (Arcinsys)
sources.title: HHStAW Fonds 557: Der Hessische Datenschutzbeauftragte (fonds description)
sources.quote: Am 7. Oktober 1970 verabschiedete der Hessische Landtag das 'Datenschutzgesetz' (GVBl. I S. 625).
sources.note: Translation: 'On 7 October 1970 the Hessian Landtag passed the Data Protection Act (GVBl. I p. 625).' The same page gives entry into force as 13.10.1970, says the law covered state authorities and bodies under state supervision (§ 1), and names the introduction of automated data processing (ADV) in the state administration as the occasion. Page date is the last accession year listed (2018-2024).

sources.institution: Der Hessische Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit (HBDI)
sources.title: Geschichte des Datenschutzes
sources.quote: Das Hessische Datenschutzgesetz von 1970 war das erste Datenschutzgesetz deutschland- und weltweit. Es reagierte auf die zunehmende Automatisierung der Datenverarbeitung.
sources.note: Translation: 'The Hessian Data Protection Act of 1970 was the first data protection law in Germany and worldwide. It responded to the increasing automation of data processing.' Page undated; year approximate.

sources.institution: Der Hessische Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit (HBDI) - lecture by CJEU judge Thomas von Danwitz
sources.title: Datenschutz in Hessen und Europa (Festvortrag, 50 Jahre Datenschutz in Hessen, 6 October 2022)
sources.quote: Nimmt man den Text des Datenschutzgesetzes vom 7.10.1970 sowie die über seine Genese Auskunft gebenden Berichte der Lesungen des Hessischen Landtags vom 8. Juli und vom 30. September 1970
sources.note: Translation: 'Taking the text of the Data Protection Act of 7.10.1970 and the reports of the Hessian Landtag's readings of 8 July and 30 September 1970 that document its genesis...'. The Hessian archive says the Landtag 'passed' the act on 7 October; 7 October 1970 is the date the act bears, and the BfDI dates the event to 30 September 1970, the later of the two Landtag readings cited here. Entry into force on 13 October 1970 is confirmed by the Baden-Württemberg DPA (https://www.baden-wuerttemberg.datenschutz.de/50-jahre-datenschutz-in-hessen/: 'Heute vor 50 Jahren, am 13.10.1970, trat das weltweit erste Datenschutzgesetz für die öffentliche Verwaltung in Kraft').

events.locationNote: The Hessian Landtag sits in the former ducal Stadtschloss on Schlossplatz, Wiesbaden.

events.title: Willi Birkelbach becomes the first data protection commissioner
events.place: Hessischer Landtag (Stadtschloss), Wiesbaden, Hesse, West Germany
events.summary: On 8 June 1971 the Hessian Landtag, on the state government's proposal, elected Willi Birkelbach as Hesse's data protection commissioner, the office created by the 1970 act; the Hessian authority describes him as the world's first data protection commissioner. From the start, anyone who believed a covered public body had mishandled their data could appeal to the commissioner (§ 11 of the 1970 act). His successor, the Frankfurt law professor Spiros Simitis, who had helped draft the 1970 act, held the office from 18 June 1975 to 22 October 1991.
events.significance: Data protection is born with an independent watchdog attached: a person, not just a rulebook, to whom individuals can complain.

sources.institution: Der Hessische Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit (HBDI)
sources.title: Geschichte des Datenschutzes
sources.quote: Der weltweit erste Datenschutzbeauftragte war Willi Birkelbach, der am 8. Juni 1971 vom Hessischen Landtag auf Vorschlag der Landesregierung gewählt wurde.
sources.note: Translation: 'The world's first data protection commissioner was Willi Birkelbach, who was elected by the Hessian Landtag on 8 June 1971 on the proposal of the state government.'

sources.institution: Hessisches Landesarchiv / Hessisches Hauptstaatsarchiv Wiesbaden (Arcinsys)
sources.title: HHStAW Fonds 557: Der Hessische Datenschutzbeauftragte (fonds description)
sources.quote: Bereits im Datenschutzgesetz von 1970 war das Recht aller Betroffenen auf Anrufung des Datenschutzbeauftragten enthalten (GVBl. I S. 625, § 11).
sources.note: Translation: 'The 1970 Data Protection Act already contained the right of all data subjects to appeal to the data protection commissioner (GVBl. I p. 625, § 11).'

sources.institution: Der Hessische Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit (HBDI)
sources.title: Trauer um den früheren Hessischen Datenschutzbeauftragten Prof. Dr. Spiros Simitis
sources.quote: In dieser frühen Phase des Datenschutzes war er 16 Jahre lang, vom 18. Juni 1975 bis zum 22. Oktober 1991, der zweite Hessische Beauftragte für Datenschutz.
sources.note: Translation: 'In this early phase of data protection he was, for 16 years, from 18 June 1975 to 22 October 1991, the second Hessian Data Protection Commissioner.' The same press release: 'Zudem hat er auch die Konzeption und Formulierung des Hessischen Datenschutzgesetzes vom 7. Oktober 1970 unterstützt' (he also supported the conception and drafting of the act).

events.title: US Fair Credit Reporting Act regulates the credit bureaus
events.summary: The Fair Credit Reporting Act was approved on 26 October 1970 as Title VI of Public Law 91-508, a statute whose earlier titles imposed record-keeping and currency-reporting duties on banks. It found a need to ensure that consumer reporting agencies act with 'a respect for the consumer's right to privacy', required them to adopt reasonable procedures for the confidentiality, accuracy, relevancy and proper use of information, and limited disclosure of consumer reports to purposes specified in the Act. The Federal Trade Commission enforces it.
events.significance: The first US law aimed at a private data industry, it treated a dossier compiled about a person as something that person could see, dispute and restrict.

sources.institution: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo), United States Statutes at Large vol. 84
sources.title: Public Law 91-508, October 26, 1970, 84 Stat. 1114 (Title VI - Consumer Credit Reporting)
sources.quote: There is a need to insure that consumer reporting agencies exercise their grave responsibilities with fairness, impartiality, and a respect for the consumer's right to privacy.
sources.note: Section 602(a)(4) of the new Title VI. The scanned statute (OCR) also shows 'Approved October 26, 1970' and the Title VI effective date of 180 days after enactment; Titles I-II of the same public law are the bank record-keeping and currency-reporting provisions later known as the Bank Secrecy Act.

sources.institution: U.S. Federal Trade Commission
sources.title: Fair Credit Reporting Act (Legal Library: Statutes)
sources.quote: Information in a consumer report cannot be provided to anyone who does not have a purpose specified in the Act.
sources.note: The same page notes the Commission 'retains all its enforcement authority' after Dodd-Frank moved most rulemaking to the CFPB. Page undated; date is access year.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the US Capitol, seat of the Congress that passed the act.

events.title: Sweden's Data Act: the first national data protection law
events.summary: Sweden's Datalag (SFS 1973:289) was issued on 11 May 1973 after the Riksdag adopted the government's bill that spring. It barred anyone from setting up or keeping a computerised personal register without the permission of a new authority, Datainspektionen (the Data Inspection Board), which was established from 1 July 1973; the permit provisions took effect a year later, after a constitutional amendment. The Liberal member of parliament Kerstin Anér was a leading advocate.
events.significance: The first nation-wide data protection law put a licensing regulator between every personal register and the people in it.

sources.institution: Sveriges riksdag (open data, Svensk författningssamling)
sources.title: Datalag (1973:289)
sources.quote: Utfärdad: 1973-05-11
sources.note: 'Issued: 1973-05-11'. The page also records 'Upphävd: 1998-10-24' (repealed 24 October 1998). The statutory text shown is the consolidated version after later amendments (e.g. Lag 1982:446 split licence and permit), not the 1973 wording. Human-readable page: https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/svensk-forfattningssamling/datalag-1973289_sfs-1973-289/

sources.institution: Svensk Juristtidning (1979), p. 497 - Jan Freese, director-general of Datainspektionen
sources.title: Datainspektionen
sources.quote: I samband därmed beslöts att en särskild myndighet, datainspek tionen, skulle inrättas fr. o. m. den 1 juli 1973. Samtidigt trädde reglerna i datalagen om tillsyn över personregister i kraft. De bestämmelser som avser tillståndsfrågor trädde i kraft först ett år senare då grundlagsändring skett.
sources.note: Translation: 'At the same time it was decided that a special authority, the Data Inspection Board, would be established from 1 July 1973. At the same time the Data Act's rules on supervision of personal registers came into force. The provisions on permits came into force only a year later, once a constitutional amendment had been made.' The line-break hyphen in 'datainspek tionen' is as printed on the digitised page.

sources.institution: Internetmuseum (Stiftelsen för internetinfrastruktur)
sources.title: Sverige blir först i världen med att införa en nationell datalag
sources.quote: Den drivande politikern, som i debatter och i riksdagsmotioner talar sig varm för behovet av att skydda medborgarnas personliga integritet, är folkpartisten Kerstin Anér.
sources.note: Translation: 'The driving politician, who argued warmly in debates and parliamentary motions for the need to protect citizens' personal integrity, was the Liberal Kerstin Anér.' The page also says the new Data Act provided that no personal register could be set up or kept without the Data Inspection Board's permission.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the Riksdag building on Helgeandsholmen, Stockholm.

events.title: HEW report proposes a Code of Fair Information Practice
events.place: U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: In July 1973 the Secretary's Advisory Committee on Automated Personal Data Systems, chaired by the computer scientist Willis Ware, published 'Records, Computers and the Rights of Citizens' (DHEW Publication No. (OS) 73-94). It recommended a federal 'Code of Fair Information Practice' for all automated personal data systems, resting on five principles, beginning with 'There must be no personal data record keeping systems whose very existence is secret.' The committee also opposed a standard universal identifier and urged steps to curb the drift of the Social Security number toward becoming one.
events.significance: The founding text of the fair information practice principles - and it already said that in trading privacy for a benefit 'both parties to the exchange should participate in setting the terms'.

sources.institution: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE)
sources.title: Records, Computers and the Rights of Citizens (full text of the 1973 report)
sources.quote: Although there is nothing inherently unfair in trading some measure of privacy for a benefit, both parties to the exchange should participate in setting the terms.
sources.note: Summary and Recommendations section. The same page states: 'the report recommends the enactment of a Federal "Code of Fair Information Practice" for all automated personal data systems. The Code rests on five basic principles...' and that it 'opposes the establishment of such an identification scheme at this time.'

sources.institution: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Privacy and Civil Liberties
sources.title: Overview of the Privacy Act of 1974 (2020 edition): Introduction
sources.quote: To address these risks, the HEW Report developed what it called a “code of fair information practices,” now more commonly called the Fair Information Practice Principles, or FIPPs.
sources.note: Gives the full citation, DHEW Publication No. (OS) 73-94 (July 1973), and credits the FIPPs to committee chairman Willis Ware, executive director David B. H. Martin and associate director Carole Parsons. DOJ's own PDF of the report (justice.gov/opcl/docs/rec-com-rights.pdf) returned HTTP 401 to scripts.

events.locationNote: Approximate coordinates of HEW's headquarters on Independence Avenue SW, Washington, D.C. (today's Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building).

events.title: US Privacy Act puts fair information practices into federal law
events.summary: The Privacy Act of 1974 (Public Law 93-579, 88 Stat. 1896) was approved on 31 December 1974 and took effect on 27 September 1975 as the principal law governing how US federal agencies handle personal information. Congress passed it in the final week of the 93rd Congress, in the wake of Watergate and COINTELPRO, relying on the HEW report's code of fair information practices. President Gerald Ford's signing statement, released at Vail, Colorado, called it 'an historic beginning'; the act also created an advisory Privacy Protection Study Commission.
events.significance: The first national statute to codify the fair information practices - but only for the federal government, leaving the private sector to later, piecemeal laws.

sources.institution: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Privacy and Civil Liberties
sources.title: Overview of the Privacy Act of 1974 (2020 edition): Introduction
sources.quote: The Privacy Act of 1974, Pub Law No. 93-579, 88 Stat 1896 (Dec. 31, 1974), codified at 5 U.S.C. § 552a (2018), went into effect on September 27, 1975
sources.note: The same page: 'Enacted in the wake of the Watergate and the Counterintelligence Program (COINTELPRO) scandals' and 'The Act was passed in great haste during the final week of the Ninety-Third United States Congress.'

sources.institution: The American Presidency Project, University of California, Santa Barbara
sources.title: Gerald R. Ford, Statement on Signing the Privacy Act of 1974
sources.quote: The Privacy Act of 1974 signified an historic beginning by codifying fundamental principles to safeguard personal privacy in the collection and handling of recorded personal information by Federal agencies.
sources.note: Editorial note on the page: 'As enacted, S. 3418, approved December 31, 1974, is Public Law 93-579 (88 Stat. 1896). The statement was released at Vail, Colo.' Ford also refers to 'the [Privacy Protection Study] Commission created by this law'.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the US Capitol (Congress). Ford's signing statement was released at Vail, Colorado.

events.title: Le Monde exposes SAFARI, a plan to link files on every French citizen
events.place: Le Monde newsroom, rue des Italiens, Paris, France
events.summary: On 21 March 1974 Le Monde published Philippe Boucher's article '"Safari" ou la chasse aux Français', describing an Iris-80 computer being brought into service for the Interior Ministry and the SAFARI operation for the individual identification of all 52 million French people. Citing a very senior magistrate, the article reported that police services held some 100 million index cards in 400 files. By a decree of 8 November 1974 the President charged a commission attached to the Minister of Justice with proposing, within six months, measures to ensure that computerisation respected private life and individual and public liberties; its report was signed in Paris on 27 June 1975.
events.significance: A single newspaper story about a master identifier turned computerised record-linking into a national political scandal, and France's data protection law followed.

sources.institution: Le Monde (archives)
sources.title: Philippe Boucher, '"Safari" ou la chasse aux Français'
sources.quote: L'appareil employé pour engranger les données de l'opération Safari, qui concerne l'identification individuelle de l'ensemble des 52 millions de Français, a une contenance de 2 milliards d'octets (1) ; celle de l'ordinateur du ministère de l'intérieur est de 3,2 milliards d'octets.
sources.note: Translation: 'The machine used to store the data of the Safari operation, which concerns the individual identification of all 52 million French people, has a capacity of 2 billion bytes; that of the Interior Ministry's computer is 3.2 billion bytes.' Byline on the page: 'Par PHILIPPE BOUCHER.' The opening paragraphs (Iris-80 at rue Jules-Breton; '100 millions de fiches, réparties dans 400 fichiers') are visible before the subscriber wall.

sources.institution: Commission Informatique et libertés / La Documentation française (PDF hosted by CNIL)
sources.title: Rapport de la Commission Informatique et libertés (décret n° 74.938 du 8 novembre 1974)
sources.quote: Le Président de la République a chargé, par décret du 8 novembre 1974, une commission instituée auprès du Garde des Sceaux
sources.note: Translation: 'By decree of 8 November 1974 the President of the Republic charged a commission established under the Minister of Justice...' The report is signed 'Paris, le 27 juin 1975' by Bernard Chenot (president), Maurice Aydalot (vice-president) and Bernard Tricot (rapporteur général), which is why it is usually called the Tricot report.

events.locationNote: Le Monde's offices were then on rue des Italiens, Paris 9e; coordinates approximate.

events.title: Church Committee exposes US intelligence surveillance of citizens
events.place: United States Senate, Capitol, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: The Senate created the Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities, chaired by Senator Frank Church, by a resolution passed on 27 January 1975. Its investigators uncovered the NSA's SHAMROCK and MINARET programmes, which monitored wire communications to and from the United States, and documented the FBI's COINTELPRO. The final report, issued on 29 April 1976, concluded that intelligence agencies had 'undermined the constitutional rights of citizens' and made 96 recommendations.
events.significance: It showed that the state's appetite for data about citizens needed legal walls, and led directly to permanent intelligence oversight and FISA.

sources.institution: United States Senate (Historical Office)
sources.title: Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities (The Church Committee)
sources.quote: “Intelligence agencies have undermined the constitutional rights of citizens,” the final report concluded, “primarily because checks and balances designed by the framers of the Constitution to assure accountability have not been applied.”
sources.note: The same page gives 'Resolution passed : Jan 27, 1975', states 'the committee published its final report on April 29, 1976', names SHAMROCK and MINARET, and says 'The final report included 96 recommendations'. Page undated; date is access year.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the US Capitol; the committee sat in the Senate office buildings nearby.

events.title: West Germany's Federal Data Protection Act
events.summary: The first version of the Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG), titled 'Gesetz zum Schutz vor Missbrauch personenbezogener Daten bei der Datenverarbeitung', was adopted on 27 January 1977. It made processing of personal data lawful only with the data subject's consent or where the act or another legal provision permitted it, and covered companies as well as public bodies. The act established a Federal Data Protection Commissioner; the first, the legal scholar Hans Peter Bull, took office on 14 February 1978.
events.significance: A national law applied the consent-or-legal-basis rule to private companies as well as the state, the template later generalised across Europe.

sources.institution: Die Bundesbeauftragte für den Datenschutz und die Informationsfreiheit (BfDI)
sources.title: Datenschutz-Garten: Die Geschichte des Datenschutzes
sources.quote: Unter dem Titel „Gesetz zum Schutz vor Missbrauch personenbezogener Daten bei der Datenverarbeitung“ wurde am 27. Januar 1977 die erste Fassung des deutschen Bundesdatenschutzgesetzes verabschiedet.
sources.note: Translation: 'Under the title "Act for Protection against Misuse of Personal Data in Data Processing" the first version of the German Federal Data Protection Act was adopted on 27 January 1977.' The page also says processing was allowed only with consent or where the BDSG or another legal provision allowed it, that it was meant to stop 'staatliche Stellen, aber auch Unternehmen' helping themselves to personal data, and: 'Der erste Verantwortliche für diese Aufgabe war der Rechtswissenschaftler Hans Peter Bull, der am 14. Februar 1978 in sein Amt eingeführt wurde.' The page's section heading reads '28. Januar 1977' while its text says 27 January; the statute is dated 27 January 1977 (BGBl. I 1977 S. 201).

sources.institution: Bundeszentrale für politische Bildung (bpb)
sources.title: 27. Januar 1977: Das Bundesdatenschutzgesetz wird verabschiedet
sources.quote: Die Datenverarbeitung war nur dann zulässig, wenn die betroffene Person darin einwilligte oder das Bundesdatenschutzgesetz oder eine andere Rechtsvorschrift dies erlaubte.
sources.note: Translation: 'Data processing was only lawful if the person concerned consented or the BDSG or another legal provision permitted it.'

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the Bundeshaus in Bonn, then seat of the Bundestag.

events.title: US Privacy Protection Study Commission reports on the private sector
events.summary: The Privacy Protection Study Commission, created by the Privacy Act of 1974, transmitted 'Personal Privacy in an Information Society' to President Jimmy Carter on 12 July 1977. Congress had asked it to recommend how far the Privacy Act's principles should apply to organisations other than federal agencies; its chapters covered credit, banking, mailing lists, insurance, employment, medical care and other record-keeping relationships. It proposed three objectives for national policy, the first 'to create a proper balance between what an individual is expected to divulge to a record-keeping organization and what he seeks in return'.
events.significance: It framed privacy as a two-sided bargain between individual and record-keeper - the exchange that person-proffered terms later try to make explicit - but most of its private-sector proposals were never enacted.

sources.institution: Privacy Protection Study Commission (text hosted by EPIC archive)
sources.title: Personal Privacy in an Information Society, Chapter 1: Introduction
sources.quote: to create a proper balance between what an individual is expected to divulge to a record- keeping organization and what he seeks in return (to minimize intrusiveness);
sources.note: The page's note to reader: 'This is Chapter 1 of Personal Privacy in an Information Society: The Report of the Privacy Protection Study Commission transmitted to President Jimmy Carter on July 12, 1977.' The stray space in 'record- keeping' is as on the page.

sources.institution: U.S. Department of Education, ERIC
sources.title: ED144554 - Personal Privacy in an Information Society. Final Report.
sources.quote: Recommendations were made to the President and Congress on the extent to which the principles of the Privacy Act of 1974 should be applied to organizations other than Federal Executive agencies
sources.note: Catalogue abstract; lists chapters on the consumer-credit, depository, mailing-list, insurance, employment and medical-care relationships.

events.locationNote: The commission was based in Washington, D.C.; coordinates are the city centre.

events.title: France's Informatique et Libertés law creates the CNIL
events.summary: Law no. 78-17 of 6 January 1978 on data processing, files and liberties opens with the declaration that computing 'must be at the service of every citizen' and must not infringe human identity, human rights, private life or individual or public liberties. It created the Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés (CNIL), which describes itself as France's first independent administrative authority. The CNIL links the law's passage to the debate that followed the SAFARI project.
events.significance: It fixed a principle - technology in the service of the citizen - and an independent regulator that shaped European data protection down to the GDPR.

sources.institution: Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés (CNIL)
sources.title: La loi Informatique et Libertés
sources.quote: L'informatique doit être au service de chaque citoyen. Son développement doit s'opérer dans le cadre de la coopération internationale. Elle ne doit porter atteinte ni à l'identité humaine, ni aux droits de l'homme, ni à la vie privée, ni aux libertés individuelles ou publiques.
sources.note: Article 1 of 'Loi n° 78-17 du 6 janvier 1978 relative à l'informatique, aux fichiers et aux libertés' as reproduced by the CNIL. Translation: 'Information technology must be at the service of every citizen. Its development must take place within the framework of international cooperation. It must not infringe human identity, human rights, private life, or individual or public liberties.' Légifrance (JORFTEXT000000886460) returned HTTP 403 to scripts.

sources.institution: Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés (CNIL)
sources.title: Informatique et Libertés : retour sur la création de la CNIL pendant le mandat du Président Valéry Giscard d'Estaing
sources.quote: Cette loi, qui a par la suite évolué, a posé la première pierre d’une sécurité nouvelle pour la protection de la vie privée des citoyens français et permis la création de la CNIL, première autorité administrative indépendante en France.
sources.note: The same page: 'Face au débat relatif aux enjeux émergents pour la vie privée et les libertés individuelles suite, notamment, à l’annonce du projet SAFARI, la loi Informatique et Libertés est votée en 1978.' Published after Giscard d'Estaing's death on 2 December 2020; exact day not shown.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the Palais Bourbon (National Assembly), Paris.

events.title: Austria makes data protection a constitutional fundamental right
events.summary: Austria's Datenschutzgesetz (DSG), federal law of 18 October 1978, was published in the Bundesgesetzblatt on 28 November 1978 as BGBl. Nr. 565/1978. Its first article, a constitutional provision headed 'Grundrecht auf Datenschutz' (fundamental right to data protection), gave everyone a claim to the confidentiality of personal data concerning them where they have an interest worthy of protection, plus rights of access to automatically processed data. Most of the act came into force on 1 January 1980.
events.significance: One of the first constitutional-rank rights to data protection, recasting information about a person as something that person holds a right over.

sources.institution: Republik Österreich, Rechtsinformationssystem des Bundes (RIS) - Bundesgesetzblatt
sources.title: BGBl. Nr. 565/1978: Bundesgesetz vom 18. Oktober 1978 über den Schutz personenbezogener Daten (Datenschutzgesetz - DSG)
sources.quote: Jedermann hat Anspruch auf Geheimhal-tung der ihn betreffenden personenbezogenen Daten,soweit er daran ein schutzwürdiges Interesse,insbesondere im Hinblick auf Achtung seines Privat-und Familienlebens, hat.
sources.note: § 1(1), under 'Artikel 1 (Verfassungsbestimmung) GRUNDRECHT AUF DATENSCHUTZ'. Hyphens and missing spaces are from the scanned PDF's text layer (printed: 'Geheimhaltung', 'Privat- und Familienlebens'). Translation: 'Everyone has a claim to the confidentiality of personal data concerning him, insofar as he has an interest worthy of protection, in particular with regard to respect for his private and family life.' The gazette header reads 'Ausgegeben am 28. November 1978'; § 58(1) sets entry into force at 1 January 1980 unless otherwise provided.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the Austrian Parliament building on the Ringstraße, Vienna.

events.title: Norway's Personal Data Registers Act and the Datatilsynet
events.summary: The Storting adopted the Personal Data Registers Act (personregisterloven) on 9 June 1978, after two government inquiries including NOU 1975: 10 on public personal-data systems. Before it could take effect, regulations had to be drafted and a Data Inspectorate (Datatilsynet) set up; a working group did both so that the law could enter into force with its regulations on 1 January 1980. In the same year, 1978, Denmark, France and Austria also legislated.
events.significance: Part of the 1978-79 wave that turned data protection from a Hessian and Swedish experiment into a European norm with a licensing regulator in each country.

sources.institution: Lov & Data (Lovdata) - article by Arve Føyen, first office head of Datatilsynet 1979-1982
sources.title: Personvernlovgivning fra 1970-tallet og til i dag

events.title: FISA requires warrants for foreign-intelligence wiretaps
events.summary: President Jimmy Carter signed the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (S. 1566, Public Law 95-511) on 25 October 1978. In his words, the bill required 'for the first time, a prior judicial warrant for all electronic surveillance for foreign intelligence or counterintelligence purposes in the United States in which communications of U.S. persons might be intercepted.' The Senate Historical Office describes FISA as one of the reforms that followed the Church Committee, with warrants to be sought from a newly formed FISA Court.
events.significance: The surveillance wall of the 1970s was procedural - a judge between the state and the wire - and it would be tested again when data moved online.

events.title: Luxembourg regulates computerised personal data
events.place: Chambre des Députés, Luxembourg City, Luxembourg
events.summary: Luxembourg's law of 31 March 1979 regulating the use of nominative data in computer processing required prior authorisation from the Minister of Justice, on the advice of a consultative commission, for creating and operating any personal-data bank. It was substantially amended in 1992 and replaced by the law of 2 August 2002 transposing the EU directive.
events.significance: Even a small state adopted the licensing model in the first decade, showing how quickly the data-bank fear of the 1970s became law across Western Europe.

events.title: OECD adopts the Privacy Guidelines and their eight principles
events.place: OECD headquarters, Château de la Muette, Paris, France
events.summary: On 23 September 1980 the Council of the OECD adopted its Recommendation concerning Guidelines governing the Protection of Privacy and Transborder Flows of Personal Data, which became applicable the same day. Developed by a group of government experts chaired by Justice M. D. Kirby of the Australian Law Reform Commission, the guidelines set out eight basic principles of national application, from collection limitation to accountability, and asked member countries to keep transborder flows of personal data 'uninterrupted and secure'. Unlike the Council of Europe's convention, they are not legally binding.
events.significance: The eight principles became the shared vocabulary of data protection worldwide - written for organisations to follow, with the individual cast as a participant rather than a party who sets terms.

events.title: Convention 108, the first binding international data protection treaty
events.place: Council of Europe, Palais de l'Europe, Strasbourg, France
events.summary: The Council of Europe's Convention for the Protection of Individuals with regard to Automatic Processing of Personal Data (ETS No. 108) was opened for signature in Strasbourg on 28 January 1981. Its purpose is to secure for every individual, whatever their nationality or residence, respect for their right to privacy with regard to automatic processing of personal data, which it calls 'data protection'. First signed by seven states, it entered into force in 1985; in 2006 the Committee of Ministers designated 28 January as Data Protection Day.
events.significance: Data protection became a treaty obligation that any state, in Europe or beyond, could join - and 28 January is still celebrated as Data Protection Day.

events.title: Census judgment establishes 'informational self-determination'
events.summary: Citizens' initiatives and public figures had called for a boycott of the West German census set for 27 April 1983, with slogans such as 'Meine Daten gehören mir' ('My data belongs to me'), and the Federal Constitutional Court suspended the count by injunction. In its judgment of 15 December 1983 (1 BvR 209/83 and others) the First Senate held that, in the context of modern data processing, the general right of personality protects the individual against the unlimited collection, storage, use and sharing of personal data and gives each person the authority, in principle, to decide on the disclosure and use of their data. It voided the census act's provisions for passing data to population registers and required further procedural safeguards; the census was finally held in 1987.
events.significance: The court turned privacy from a wall around the home into a person's right to decide who knows what about them - the conceptual root of person-set data terms.

sources.institution: Bundesverfassungsgericht (Federal Constitutional Court of Germany)
sources.title: Judgment of the First Senate of 15 December 1983, 1 BvR 209, 269, 362, 420, 440, 484/83 (Census Act) - English translation
sources.quote: This fundamental right confers upon the individual the authority to, in principle, decide themselves on the disclosure and use of their personal data.
sources.note: Headnote 1. The reasons add: 'A societal order, and its underlying legal order, would not be compatible with the right to informational self-determination if citizens were no longer able to tell who knows what kind of personal information about them, at what time and on which occasion.' Operative part: '§ 9(1) to (3) of the 1983 Census Act is not compatible with Article 2(1) in conjunction with Article 1(1) of the Basic Law, and is thus void.'

events.title: UK Data Protection Act creates the Data Protection Registrar
events.place: Palace of Westminster, London, United Kingdom
events.summary: The Data Protection Act 1984 (c. 35) received Royal Assent on 12 July 1984 as 'An Act to regulate the use of automatically processed information relating to individuals'. Its first schedule set out eight data protection principles, beginning with the rule that information in personal data be obtained, and the data processed, 'fairly and lawfully'. It created a Data Protection Registrar and a Data Protection Tribunal; Eric Howe was Registrar from 1984 to 1994, heading an office of ten people at the start.
events.significance: Britain's first data protection law regulated computer users through a public register, the ancestor of today's Information Commissioner's Office.

events.title: ECPA extends US wiretap law to email and stored data
events.summary: The Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1986 (Public Law 99-508) was approved on 21 October 1986 to amend title 18 'with respect to the interception of certain communications, other forms of surveillance, and for other purposes'. It updated the Federal Wiretap Act of 1968, which had covered interception over 'hard' telephone lines but not computer and other digital communications. Its Title II, the Stored Communications Act, protects the contents of files stored by service providers and records they hold about subscribers.
events.significance: The first US attempt to carry the sealed-letter idea into computer networks - written before the web, and still governing much of email today.

events.title: A newspaper prints a Supreme Court nominee's video rentals
events.summary: While Judge Robert Bork's nomination to the US Supreme Court was before the Senate, the Washington City Paper issue of 25 September - 1 October 1987 carried Michael Dolan's 'The Bork Tapes', an analysis of the videotapes rented on the Bork household's account at a Washington video store. Dolan counted '146 rentals, including repeats – in less than two years'; the list, leaked by a store clerk, revealed nothing particularly salacious. The intrusion drew bipartisan anger in Congress.
events.significance: It showed legislators in person how a routine commercial record can expose a mind - the reasoning behind protecting what people read and watch.

events.title: Video Privacy Protection Act follows the Bork tapes
events.summary: The Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988 (Public Law 100-618), approved on 5 November 1988, amended title 18 'to preserve personal privacy with respect to the rental, purchase, or delivery of video tapes or similar audio visual materials'. A video tape service provider that knowingly discloses information identifying a customer as having requested or obtained specific video materials is liable to that customer, unless an exception applies - one being disclosure with the consumer's informed, written consent given at the time the disclosure is sought. In 2011 the first class action under the act against an online service, Hulu, was brought, and the court held that streaming services could be covered.
events.significance: A consent rule attached to one specific disclosure at the moment it is sought - a narrow, early form of the person setting the terms for their own data.

events.title: US Congress regulates government computer matching
events.summary: The Computer Matching and Privacy Protection Act of 1988 (Public Law 100-503), approved on 18 October 1988, amended the Privacy Act 'to ensure privacy, integrity, and verification of data disclosed for computer matching' and to establish Data Integrity Boards within federal agencies. Its first operative section required written matching agreements before agency records could be disclosed for a computer matching programme. The Justice Department describes it as extending the Privacy Act's fair information practice protections to agencies' computer matching.
events.significance: Lawmakers recognised that joining databases, not only collecting data, was itself a privacy harm - a problem that AI-scale data fusion has multiplied.

events.title: Online protest kills Lotus MarketPlace: Households
events.place: Lotus Development Corporation, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States
events.summary: On 10 April 1990 Lotus Development Corporation announced Lotus MarketPlace: Households, a CD-ROM made with the credit bureau Equifax that would have put names, addresses, demographic and purchase-behaviour data on 120 million US consumers onto desktop computers. After the Wall Street Journal reported on it in November 1990, opposition was mobilised 'individual by individual, on "the net"', and more than 30,000 people asked to have their names removed. On 23 January 1991 Lotus and Equifax cancelled the product, citing consumer concerns and the cost of addressing privacy issues.
events.significance: One of the first times networked individuals, not regulators, stopped a data product - a preview of people asserting their own terms online.

events.summary: In 1993 Québec's National Assembly adopted An Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector (S.Q. 1993, c. 17; R.S.Q., c. events.significance: It brought European-style data protection for companies to North America, a jurisdiction the US federal system never matched.

events.title: New Zealand's Privacy Act applies one set of principles to government and business
events.summary: New Zealand's Privacy Act 1993 came into force on 1 July 1993. Its long title described it as an Act to promote and protect individual privacy 'in general accordance with' the OECD's 1980 privacy guidelines, establishing principles for the collection, use and disclosure of personal information by public and private sector agencies alike. The New Zealand Law Commission later wrote that it was enacted to balance the state's wish to make greater use of personal information, especially for data matching, with individual privacy.
events.significance: An early example of the OECD principles written directly into one law covering every organisation, public or private.

myths.claim: Data protection law began with the EU's GDPR.
myths.correction: The GDPR, applied from May 2018, came nearly half a century after the first data protection statute: Hesse's act of 1970. myths.claim: The fair information practice principles were invented by the OECD in 1980.
myths.correction: The OECD Guidelines codified principles already in circulation. The US HEW advisory committee proposed a 'Code of Fair Information Practice' with five principles in July 1973; the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers adopted resolutions on data banks in 1973 and 1974; and Hesse, Sweden, West Germany, France and others had already legislated. The OECD's own explanatory memorandum surveys this earlier work.
